entities.name: Methodios I of Constantinople
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Methodios I (born c. 788/790 in Syracuse, Sicily; died June 14, 847, Constantinople), served as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from March 11, 843, until his death. His brief but pivotal patriarchate definitively concluded the Second Iconoclasm, a century-long theological and political struggle that had deeply fractured the Byzantine Empire. As a staunch defender of icon veneration, Methodios played a crucial role in restoring orthodoxy and securing the veneration of sacred images, thereby shaping the visual and spiritual landscape of the Eastern Orthodox Church for over a millennium. His elevation marked the formal triumph of the iconophile faction, a victory celebrated annually as the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'.

Before his patriarchate, Methodios endured significant persecution under the iconoclast emperors, including a period of imprisonment on the island of Principo. His theological acumen and unwavering commitment to icon veneration, cultivated through monastic life, made him a leading figure in the iconophile resistance. Upon the death of Emperor Theophilos in 842, his empress regent, Theodora, herself an iconophile, orchestrated Methodios's ascension to the patriarchal throne, replacing the last iconoclast patriarch, John VII Grammatikos. Methodios immediately convened a synod in 843, which formally reaffirmed the decrees of the Second Council of Nicaea (787) and anathematized leading iconoclasts. This synod's decisions were publicly proclaimed on March 11, 843, in a grand procession that restored icons to the Hagia Sophia, an event commemorated as the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy'.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Methodios I's patriarchate definitively ended the Second Iconoclasm in 843, restoring icon veneration and establishing the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' as a foundational event for Eastern Orthodoxy. His actions solidified the visual and theological identity of a major world religion for over a millennium.
